source_batch.unit_label: Module D unit 5 (courseware unit 30): compliance culture, GRC framework and whistle-blowing

facts.statement: Compliance culture (courseware): "workplace behaviour that naturally meets ethical and legal norms"; culture is the foundation that shapes employee decisions in the moment, informing decisions through explicit and implicit reference to organisational values, norms and assumptions. A strong compliance culture ensures adherence to fair practice codes, manages conflicts of interest and treats customers fairly; compliance goes beyond what is legally binding to integrity and ethical conduct. Culture should be visibly embraced by senior management, built into hiring and training, ideally linked to pay and promotions, and measured with the right metrics over time. Benefits: low organisational and individual risk; low reputational risk; employee confidence; ability to attract and retain talent; better transparency and decisions; better relationships with regulators and stakeholders; enhanced valuation among investors. Banks that did stress testing reported that the most important benefit of complying with stress testing principles was better informed capital planning decisions and a forward-looking view of the organisation's risks. Signs of poor culture: focus on short-term profitability and personal interests; dominance of individuals in decision forums and lack of challenge; sub-cultures not aligned with the organisation (especially after acquisitions or mergers); adherence to the letter but not the spirit of law (tick-box attitude); treating internal control or risk management as an irritant; ineffective incentive structures; covering up problems; following the market attitude; employees not encouraged to speak up; failing to challenge the status quo. Costs of poor culture include legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss and loss of reputation; banks should convert misconduct into case studies for staff, and see proper conduct as saving the bank penalties and generating hidden earnings.

RBI penalty risk and the Indian scenario (courseware): the risk of RBI penalties arises from non-compliance with prudential and regulatory norms, integrity and market conduct, legal directions and related Acts, and internal policies and procedures approved by the bank's Board; the courseware gives many historic examples (mis-selling, KYC and AML lapses, fraud classification and reporting, cyber security, account payee cheque collection). Fear of fines should be replaced by a management system with built-in control that makes compliance an everyday practice. The courseware states that RBI introduced the designation of a Compliance Officer in banks in August 1992 on the Committee on Frauds and Malpractices in Banks (Ghosh Committee) recommendations, and that the Basel Committee issued its high level paper on compliance risk and the compliance function in banks in April 2005. A common thread in most frauds is non-adherence to internal policies and procedures. Seven elements of a compliance programme: written policies, procedures and standards of conduct; a compliance officer and committee; effective training and education; effective lines of communication; internal monitoring and auditing; enforcing standards through well-publicised disciplinary guidelines; and responding promptly to detected offences and taking corrective action.

Ten attributes regulators look for in a culture of compliance (courseware): tone at the top (senior management's engagement; cost-benefit reasoning on illegal transactions shows no culture); integration across the enterprise (credit, interest rate, market, liquidity and operational risk overlap, so compliance works with all risk areas); silos (compliance staff present when business decisions are made); power (whether the CCO is part of senior management and who wins, business or compliance); cowboys (rewards based only on financial performance without limits on risk-taking); resources (investment in compliance technology compared with business); employee buy-in (zero tolerance policy on misconduct and continuing training); a living compliance programme (tailored, tested, modified, enforced, with issues escalated); technology (automation of compliance workflow); and documentation (record keeping that proves testing and sign-off).

Minimum supervisory expectation on compliance culture: compliance starts at the top, is part of the organisation's culture, and is a shared responsibility of each staff member, with business units equally responsible for non-compliance. The RBI circular of 11 September 2020 requires the Board-approved policy to set expectations on tone from the top, accountability, incentive structure, and effective communication and challenge. The courseware elaborates: tone from the top (Board and senior management values and demonstrated actions; the Board's oversight not limited to the compliance function); accountability (senior management responsible for adherence to policy; clear demarcation of accountability of senior management, functional heads and operational heads; business as the first line of defence and internal audit as third); communication (clarity and transparency, distinguishing general standards for all staff from rules for specific groups; awareness channels for existing and new Board members, senior management and employees; process for conduct risk and a whistle-blower mechanism); incentive structure (adequate, built into decision systems and processes); and ex ante and forward looking (compliance is preventive, assessing the bank's activities beforehand to prevent non-compliant activities or transactions, unlike risk management and internal audit).
facts.locator: S01 printed p. 641; four elements confirmed by RBI_CCO_2020 paragraph 2.1

facts.statement: Compliance organisation, authority and resources (courseware): the bank organises its compliance function and sets priorities consistently with its risk management strategy and structures, and because compliance risk is closely related to certain operational risks, mechanisms ensure close cooperation between the two functions. The function has sufficient authority, stature, independence, resources and access to the Board; its responsibilities are clearly specified; its activities are subject to periodic and independent review by internal audit; management respects its independence and does not interfere. The CCO's compliance programme begins with: addressing major compliance issues on a priority basis; coordinating with the Central Audit and Inspection department to identify key compliance issues from audit findings; developing testing and monitoring procedures through Risk officers posted at regional, zonal and Field General Manager offices; reviewing the policies of functional departments based on implementation experience; and creating awareness by including at least one session on the compliance function in each training programme. On a pro-active basis the function identifies, documents and assesses the compliance risks of business activities, new products, new types of business or customer relationships and material changes in them.

Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) framework (courseware): growing regulation, business complexity and accountability lead enterprises to pursue governance, risk and compliance initiatives that are often uncoordinated and run in silos, causing duplication and rising cost. GRC has three elements: governance (the oversight role and process by which companies manage business risks, including definition and communication of corporate control, key policies, enterprise risk management, regulatory and compliance management and oversight, ethics, and evaluating performance through balanced scorecards, risk scorecards and operational dashboards); risk management (a structured process to evaluate relevant business and regulatory risks and controls and monitor mitigation, covering financial, operational, IT, brand and reputational risks); and compliance (the processes and internal controls that meet the requirements of governmental bodies, regulators, industry mandates and internal policies, made repeatable so compliance is sustained at lower cost than the first deadline project). A GRC solution is an integrated platform for standardising and managing strategic and operational risk and consolidating information from financial risk systems (credit, market and others) into an enterprise view across risk identification, assessment, response and monitoring; it may be web-based, with modules such as incident management, risk control self-assessment (RCSA), key risk indicators (KRI), issues and action plans, compliance and policy management, governance and audit management, and regulatory reports (for example Basic Indicator Approach and Standardised Approach, and other MIS). Benefits of an integrated GRC approach: a clear single reference and greater organisational effectiveness; elimination of redundant work; no duplicated software, hardware, training and rollout costs; a single version of the truth for employees, management, auditors and regulators; and a significant reduction in the cost of compliance.

Whistle-blower policy: model policy (courseware): the company gives employees freedom to report, and to tell management the facts, so that unethical, immoral or illegal work is stopped. Objectives: give employees, investors, contractors, vendors and other stakeholders a platform to raise concerns about wrongdoing; protect employees against retaliation; support ethical business; let employees report through an authorised channel operated under the audit committee. Model guidelines: every employee is responsible for raising concerns; an illegal activity not reported despite knowledge is a breach of ethical behaviour; no retaliation against the whistle-blower (retaliation includes suspension, decrease in salary, poor-quality assignments, verbal or written threats); protection covers confidentiality and generally keeping the identity confidential except where needed for investigation or law; people working alongside or representing the whistle-blower are also protected; no discrimination on salary or terms of employment; no discrimination against an employee helping the investigation; the policy does not provide compensation to the employee for participation; a person is not entitled to protection unless the concern is raised in good faith. Areas covered include harassment or discrimination, sharing of confidential information, breach of privacy, fraud, misrepresentation of financial data, illegal activity, corruption, illegal sales activity, invalid promotion, conflict of interest, trading within the company, illegal competitive behaviour and improper use of company assets. Principle of reporting: an employee who sees a violation of the code of conduct, or doubts that an illegal activity is happening or can happen, informs a superior or the legal department immediately.

Whistle-blowing process (courseware model): the whistle-blower can raise a concern in writing or verbally with the ombudsperson or CVO (a verbal complaint is written up by the ombudsperson); the ombudsperson, CVO or audit committee checks whether a breach has occurred and responds within 2 days of receiving the complaint; the whistle-blower may or may not disclose identity, a complaint without identity is still taken seriously, and identity is kept confidential in all cases; false allegations lead to strict disciplinary action; on investigation the audit committee (or CVO or ombudsperson) contacts the employee, vendor and stakeholder for information, decides the internal steps, keeps all information confidential and shares status and findings with the Board of directors, with a final report that contains all details and documentation. Alternatives to raising a concern with the manager or head of department: Human Resources, head of the department, the legal department, the Compliance Head, the CEO or CVO, and management committee members; in an urgent situation an employee can write directly to the chairman of the audit committee; a complaint received by HR is sent to the director of human resources for action. The courseware lists five reasons employees do not report unethical conduct (ACFE): no corrective action, no confidentiality of reports, retaliation by superiors, retaliation by co-workers and being unsure whom to contact. Components of a whistle-blower policy: a whistle-blower (a person who raises a concern about wrongdoing, typically from within the organisation), a wrongful or unethical practice (grave and serious, such as serious disregard of the law, crimes against human rights, corruption or compromise of values; trivial or unfounded claims should not be escalated), an authority (a defined escalation process with an independent, senior and responsible authority and confidentiality of the information and the informer) and a policy (an internal policy on access; the Corporate Governance code says the whistle-blower must have a direct access to the Chairman of the audit committee). Benefits: good governance, promotion of values and openness, a clear message that severe action will be taken against unethical acts, deterrence through fear of consequences and early alerts to defuse larger disasters.

Whistle-blowing in India as the courseware presents it: internal whistle-blowers report fraud or corruption to senior management, external ones to the media, public or law authorities. The courseware says laws on whistle-blowing and protection are inadequate and the Companies Act, 2013 provides for whistle-blowing and corporate governance through a vigil mechanism; sections 206 to 229 cover inspection, inquiry and investigation (section 208 inspector, section 210 investigation by order of the Central Government on a report of the Registrar or inspector, on a special resolution or in the public interest, section 211 Serious Fraud Investigation Office); and section 177(9) makes a whistle-blower policy compulsory for listed companies, companies accepting deposits from the public and companies that borrowed over Rs 50 crore from banks or public financial institutions. Clause 49 of the (old) SEBI listing agreement set a non-mandatory requirement of a mechanism to report concerns, safeguards against victimisation, direct access to the audit committee chairman where senior management is involved, communication within the organisation and periodic audit committee review. The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2011 (originally a 2010 Bill) replaced the 2004 Government Resolution but, as the courseware says, "has not come into force yet". The Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informers (PIDPI) Resolution, 2004, issued after the Supreme Court direction in the Satyendra Dubey case, designates the Central Vigilance Commission to receive written complaints on corruption or misuse of office in the central government and its corporations; anonymous complaints are not acted upon; the complainant's identity is not revealed unless the complainant disclosed it; a victimised complainant can apply to the designated agency for redress; a 2013 amendment authorised Chief Vigilance Officers of ministries and departments as designated authorities with the CVC supervising and monitoring complaints.

Reasons for compliance failures (courseware, from the point of view of those targeted): failure to understand the law (rules too complex); collapse in belief in the law (compliance too costly or standards unreasonable); overly legalistic regulation; regulation at odds with market incentives or cultural practices; failure to monitor; procedural injustice (people who feel unfairly treated by a regulator comply less); deterrence failure (high rewards for rule breaking and low probability of detection); failures of administrative capacity; failure to understand the problem; failure of causal relation between regulation and objective. The courseware adds that the compliance function should be independent of business, with staff having the necessary qualifications, experience and personal qualities; it should have a formal status in the bank, and for banks with business in other jurisdictions it should be structured so that local compliance issues are addressed within the bank-wide policy; the compliance policy is effective only with a clear commitment of the Board of Directors to promote values of honesty and integrity.

payload.title: Compliance culture, its benefits and warning signs
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance culture** is **workplace behaviour that naturally meets ethical and legal norms**. It shapes decisions in the moment and goes **beyond what the law requires** to **integrity and ethical conduct**. It should be **visible in senior management**, built into **hiring and training**, ideally **linked to pay and promotion**, and **measured**.

**Benefits:** **lower organisational, individual and reputational risk**; **employee confidence**; **attract and retain talent**; **better transparency and decisions**; **better regulator relationships**; **stronger valuation**.

**Signs of poor culture:** **short-term profit** focus; **dominant individuals** and **no challenge**; **sub-cultures** after mergers; **tick-box** (letter, not spirit) compliance; controls seen as an **irritant**; **ineffective incentives**; **cover-ups**; **employees afraid to speak up**; **no challenge of the status quo**.

**What banks should do:** turn misconduct into **case studies** for staff and see good conduct as **saving penalties**, a **hidden earning**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware also notes that stress-testing banks valued better capital planning and a forward-looking view of risk.

self_check.prompt_text: What is meant by a tick-box attitude?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Following the letter of the law or regulation but not its spirit.

| **Silos** | Is compliance **present when business decisions are made**? |
| **Power** | Is the **CCO part of senior management**, and who wins a dispute, business or compliance? |
| **Cowboys** | Are rewards based **only on financial performance**, with **no limits on risk-taking**? |
| **Resources** | Is compliance **funded** compared with business technology? |
| **Employee buy-in** | **Zero tolerance** for misconduct; **continuing training** |
| **Living compliance programme** | **Tailored, tested, modified, enforced**; issues **escalated** |
| **Technology** | Is compliance **automated** or on paper? |
| **Documentation** | Can the bank **prove** testing and sign-off? |

payload.title: The GRC framework
payload.core_explanation_md:
Many enterprises run **governance, risk and compliance** initiatives **separately**, which causes **silos, duplication and rising cost**. **GRC** brings them together.

| Element | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Governance** | **Oversight** by which risks are managed: **corporate controls, key policies, enterprise risk management, regulatory and compliance oversight, ethics**, and performance tracking through **balanced scorecards, risk scorecards and operational dashboards** |
| **Risk management** | A **structured process** to **evaluate business and regulatory risks and controls** and **monitor mitigation** (financial, operational, IT, brand, reputational) |
| **Compliance** | **Processes and internal controls** meeting **regulator, industry and internal requirements**, made **repeatable** so it is sustained at **lower cost** than the first deadline project |

**A GRC solution** is an **integrated platform** giving an **enterprise view** of risk across **identification, assessment, response and monitoring**. It can be **web-based**, with modules such as **incident management**, **RCSA** (risk control self-assessment), **KRI** (key risk indicators), **issues and action plans**, **compliance and policy management**, **governance and audit management** and **regulatory reports**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Treating compliance as a one-off project makes each new regulation expensive; making it repeatable lowers the cost.

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Protection for good-faith reporters is balanced by discipline for false allegations.

payload.title: The whistle-blowing process and components of a policy
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Raising a concern:** in **writing or verbally** to the **ombudsperson or CVO** (a verbal complaint is **written up** by the ombudsperson). The ombudsperson, CVO or **audit committee** checks whether a breach occurred and **responds within 2 days** of receiving the complaint.

**Identity:** the whistle-blower may or may not reveal it; either way the complaint is **taken seriously**, and the **identity is kept confidential** in all cases. **False allegations** bring **strict disciplinary action**.

**Investigation:** the committee **contacts** the employee, vendor or stakeholder, decides **internal steps**, keeps everything **confidential** and **shares status and findings with the Board**, with a **final report** holding all details and documents.

**Alternative routes:** manager or **head of department**, **HR**, **legal**, **Compliance Head**, **CEO or CVO**, **management committee members**; in an **urgent** case **write directly to the chair of the audit committee**; a complaint received by HR goes to the **director of human resources**.

**Four components of a policy:** a **whistle-blower**, a **wrongful or unethical practice** (grave and serious, not trivial), an **authority** (independent, senior, responsible; a defined escalation process) and **a policy** (with **direct access to the chair of the audit committee**).

**Five reasons staff do not report (ACFE):** **no corrective action**, **no confidentiality**, **retaliation by superiors**, **retaliation by co-workers**, **unsure whom to contact**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The audit committee chair is the escape route when senior management is the subject of the complaint.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days does the courseware model say the ombudsperson or audit committee should respond to a complaint?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within 2 days of receiving it.

payload.title: Whistle-blowing law and rules in India (courseware account)
payload.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review: statutes and circulars cited by the courseware were **not checked** against primary text, and the **Listing Agreement clause 49** it cites has been **replaced by the SEBI Listing Regulations 2015**.

**Companies Act, 2013 (as the courseware describes):** **vigil mechanism** provisions; sections **206 to 229** on **inspection, inquiry and investigation**; **section 177(9)** requires a whistle-blower policy for **listed companies**, companies **accepting public deposits** and companies **borrowing over Rs 50 crore from banks or public financial institutions**. The **Serious Fraud Investigation Office** is created under **section 211**.

**Old clause 49 (non-mandatory part):** a **mechanism to report concerns**, **safeguards against victimisation**, **direct access to the audit committee chair** where **senior management is involved**, **communication within the organisation** and **periodic audit committee review**.

**Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2011:** the courseware says it **has not come into force**; its status at the cut-off was **not verified**, so it is **not tested**.

**PIDPI Resolution, 2004** (after the **Satyendra Dubey** case): the **Central Vigilance Commission** is the **designated agency** for **written complaints** on **corruption or misuse of office** in the central government and its corporations; **anonymous complaints are not acted upon**; the **complainant's identity is not revealed** unless disclosed by the complainant; a **victimised complainant may apply for redress**; a **2013 amendment** made **Chief Vigilance Officers** designated authorities under CVC supervision.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Internal whistle-blowers report within the organisation; external ones go to the media, public or law authorities.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the PIDPI Resolution act on anonymous complaints?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, anonymous complaints are not acted upon (courseware).

payload.title: Why compliance fails
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware lists reasons from the standpoint of those the rules target:

| Reason | Point |
| --- | --- |
| **Failure to understand the law** | Requirements are **too complex** |
| **Collapse in belief in the law** | Compliance **costs too much**; standards seem **unreasonable** |
| **Overly legalistic regulation** | Technical rules that **do not relate to the purpose** lose confidence |
| **Regulation at odds with market incentives or culture** | Rules that **do not fit market practice** are obeyed less |
| **Failure to monitor** | A rule **not monitored vigorously** draws **little compliance** |
| **Procedural injustice** | People **treated unfairly** comply less |
| **Deterrence failure** | **High rewards** for breaking rules and **low chance of detection** |
| **Failures of administrative capacity** | Agencies do not provide **resources, information or support** for implementation |
| **Failure to understand the problem** | Government misreads the cause |
| **Failure of causal relation** | The rule **does not achieve its objective** |

**For banks:** an **independent** compliance function with **qualified staff** and **formal status**; **local compliance** issues in other jurisdictions handled **within the bank-wide policy**; and a **Board commitment to honesty and integrity**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Deterrence fails when detection is unlikely, which is why monitoring and enforcement matter.

self_check.prompt_text: Which reason says rules are obeyed less when people feel treated unfairly by a regulator?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Procedural injustice.

items.title: Compliance culture, its benefits and warning signs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance culture** is **workplace behaviour that naturally meets ethical and legal norms**. It shapes decisions in the moment and goes **beyond what the law requires** to **integrity and ethical conduct**. It should be **visible in senior management**, built into **hiring and training**, ideally **linked to pay and promotion**, and **measured**.

**Benefits:** **lower organisational, individual and reputational risk**; **employee confidence**; **attract and retain talent**; **better transparency and decisions**; **better regulator relationships**; **stronger valuation**.

**Signs of poor culture:** **short-term profit** focus; **dominant individuals** and **no challenge**; **sub-cultures** after mergers; **tick-box** (letter, not spirit) compliance; controls seen as an **irritant**; **ineffective incentives**; **cover-ups**; **employees afraid to speak up**; **no challenge of the status quo**.

**What banks should do:** turn misconduct into **case studies** for staff and see good conduct as **saving penalties**, a **hidden earning**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware also notes that stress-testing banks valued better capital planning and a forward-looking view of risk.

self_check.prompt_text: What is meant by a tick-box attitude?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Following the letter of the law or regulation but not its spirit.

items.title: Ten attributes of a culture of compliance
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware). What regulators look for:

| Attribute | What they ask |
| --- | --- |
| **Tone at the top** | Do leaders put compliance above deal value? |
| **Integration across the enterprise** | Does compliance work with all **risk areas** (credit, market, liquidity, operational)? |
| **Silos** | Is compliance **present when business decisions are made**? |
| **Power** | Is the **CCO part of senior management**, and who wins a dispute, business or compliance? |
| **Cowboys** | Are rewards based **only on financial performance**, with **no limits on risk-taking**? |
| **Resources** | Is compliance **funded** compared with business technology? |
| **Employee buy-in** | **Zero tolerance** for misconduct; **continuing training** |
| **Living compliance programme** | **Tailored, tested, modified, enforced**; issues **escalated** |
| **Technology** | Is compliance **automated** or on paper? |
| **Documentation** | Can the bank **prove** testing and sign-off? |

items.title: RBI's minimum supervisory expectations on compliance culture
items.core_explanation_md:
Compliance **starts at the top**, is part of the **organisation's culture** and is a **shared responsibility of every staff member**; **business units are equally responsible** for non-compliance.

**RBI circular (11 September 2020):** the Board-approved policy sets expectations on **tone from the top, accountability, incentive structure and effective communication and challenge**.

| Element | Courseware's detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Tone from the top** | Values of Board and senior management **shown in actions**; Board oversight **not limited to the compliance function** |
| **Accountability** | Senior management **responsible for adherence**; **clear demarcation** of senior management, functional and operational heads; **business is the first line, internal audit the third** |
| **Communication** | **Clear and transparent**; **general standards for all staff** distinguished from **rules for specific groups**; **awareness channels**; **conduct risk process and whistle-blower mechanism** |
| **Incentive structure** | **Built into decision systems and processes** |
| **Ex ante and forward looking** | Compliance is **preventive**, unlike risk management and internal audit |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Compliance prevents non-compliant transactions beforehand rather than detecting them afterwards.

items.title: The GRC framework
items.core_explanation_md:
Many enterprises run **governance, risk and compliance** initiatives **separately**, which causes **silos, duplication and rising cost**. **GRC** brings them together.

| Element | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Governance** | **Oversight** by which risks are managed: **corporate controls, key policies, enterprise risk management, regulatory and compliance oversight, ethics**, and performance tracking through **balanced scorecards, risk scorecards and operational dashboards** |
| **Risk management** | A **structured process** to **evaluate business and regulatory risks and controls** and **monitor mitigation** (financial, operational, IT, brand, reputational) |
| **Compliance** | **Processes and internal controls** meeting **regulator, industry and internal requirements**, made **repeatable** so it is sustained at **lower cost** than the first deadline project |

**A GRC solution** is an **integrated platform** giving an **enterprise view** of risk across **identification, assessment, response and monitoring**. It can be **web-based**, with modules such as **incident management**, **RCSA** (risk control self-assessment), **KRI** (key risk indicators), **issues and action plans**, **compliance and policy management**, **governance and audit management** and **regulatory reports**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Treating compliance as a one-off project makes each new regulation expensive; making it repeatable lowers the cost.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three elements of GRC.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Governance, risk management and compliance.

items.title: The whistle-blowing process and components of a policy
items.core_explanation_md:
**Raising a concern:** in **writing or verbally** to the **ombudsperson or CVO** (a verbal complaint is **written up** by the ombudsperson). The ombudsperson, CVO or **audit committee** checks whether a breach occurred and **responds within 2 days** of receiving the complaint.

**Identity:** the whistle-blower may or may not reveal it; either way the complaint is **taken seriously**, and the **identity is kept confidential** in all cases. **False allegations** bring **strict disciplinary action**.

**Investigation:** the committee **contacts** the employee, vendor or stakeholder, decides **internal steps**, keeps everything **confidential** and **shares status and findings with the Board**, with a **final report** holding all details and documents.

**Alternative routes:** manager or **head of department**, **HR**, **legal**, **Compliance Head**, **CEO or CVO**, **management committee members**; in an **urgent** case **write directly to the chair of the audit committee**; a complaint received by HR goes to the **director of human resources**.

**Four components of a policy:** a **whistle-blower**, a **wrongful or unethical practice** (grave and serious, not trivial), an **authority** (independent, senior, responsible; a defined escalation process) and **a policy** (with **direct access to the chair of the audit committee**).

**Five reasons staff do not report (ACFE):** **no corrective action**, **no confidentiality**, **retaliation by superiors**, **retaliation by co-workers**, **unsure whom to contact**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The audit committee chair is the escape route when senior management is the subject of the complaint.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days does the courseware model say the ombudsperson or audit committee should respond to a complaint?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within 2 days of receiving it.

items.title: Whistle-blowing law and rules in India (courseware account)
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review: statutes and circulars cited by the courseware were **not checked** against primary text, and the **Listing Agreement clause 49** it cites has been **replaced by the SEBI Listing Regulations 2015**.

**Companies Act, 2013 (as the courseware describes):** **vigil mechanism** provisions; sections **206 to 229** on **inspection, inquiry and investigation**; **section 177(9)** requires a whistle-blower policy for **listed companies**, companies **accepting public deposits** and companies **borrowing over Rs 50 crore from banks or public financial institutions**. The **Serious Fraud Investigation Office** is created under **section 211**.

**Old clause 49 (non-mandatory part):** a **mechanism to report concerns**, **safeguards against victimisation**, **direct access to the audit committee chair** where **senior management is involved**, **communication within the organisation** and **periodic audit committee review**.

**Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2011:** the courseware says it **has not come into force**; its status at the cut-off was **not verified**, so it is **not tested**.

**PIDPI Resolution, 2004** (after the **Satyendra Dubey** case): the **Central Vigilance Commission** is the **designated agency** for **written complaints** on **corruption or misuse of office** in the central government and its corporations; **anonymous complaints are not acted upon**; the **complainant's identity is not revealed** unless disclosed by the complainant; a **victimised complainant may apply for redress**; a **2013 amendment** made **Chief Vigilance Officers** designated authorities under CVC supervision.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Internal whistle-blowers report within the organisation; external ones go to the media, public or law authorities.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the PIDPI Resolution act on anonymous complaints?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, anonymous complaints are not acted upon (courseware).

items.title: Why compliance fails
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware lists reasons from the standpoint of those the rules target:

| Reason | Point |
| --- | --- |
| **Failure to understand the law** | Requirements are **too complex** |
| **Collapse in belief in the law** | Compliance **costs too much**; standards seem **unreasonable** |
| **Overly legalistic regulation** | Technical rules that **do not relate to the purpose** lose confidence |
| **Regulation at odds with market incentives or culture** | Rules that **do not fit market practice** are obeyed less |
| **Failure to monitor** | A rule **not monitored vigorously** draws **little compliance** |
| **Procedural injustice** | People **treated unfairly** comply less |
| **Deterrence failure** | **High rewards** for breaking rules and **low chance of detection** |
| **Failures of administrative capacity** | Agencies do not provide **resources, information or support** for implementation |
| **Failure to understand the problem** | Government misreads the cause |
| **Failure of causal relation** | The rule **does not achieve its objective** |

**For banks:** an **independent** compliance function with **qualified staff** and **formal status**; **local compliance** issues in other jurisdictions handled **within the bank-wide policy**; and a **Board commitment to honesty and integrity**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Deterrence fails when detection is unlikely, which is why monitoring and enforcement matter.

self_check.prompt_text: Which reason says rules are obeyed less when people feel treated unfairly by a regulator?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Procedural injustice.
